html:
At the Battle of Isandlwana on 22 January 1879, a Zulu army of about 20,000 men overran a British camp at the foot of the hill of Isandlwana and killed more than 1,300 soldiers. It was one of the worst defeats of a modern European army by an African force.

Britain had invaded the Zulu Kingdom eleven days earlier, at the start of the Anglo-Zulu War, after making demands that King Cetshwayo could not accept. The British commander, Lord Chelmsford, split his column and left the camp poorly defended. The Zulu regiments attacked in their traditional "horns of the buffalo" formation, encircling the British line, and fought through heavy rifle fire.

The same night a small British garrison held off a Zulu force at Rorke's Drift. Britain sent more troops, and in July it burned the royal kraal after the Battle of Ulundi. Cetshwayo was captured and the kingdom was broken into pieces. Isandlwana, like Adwa in Ethiopia later, stands as a symbol of African resistance to conquest.
